opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I find most interesting from that line of work. The setup is a small two-layer, attention-only transformer trained on natural language, and we were using refined versions of the local learning coefficient, which are restricted to particular components like individual attention heads and evaluated on particular kinds of data. That gives us a way of watching how complexity is distributed across the model over training.

The rough picture is that early on the model is learning simple statistics: unigrams, then bigrams, then increasingly richer n-gram-like patterns, including skip n-grams where tokens don't have to be adjacent. We call that family "multigrams." What we see is that the attention heads start out looking fairly similar and then differentiate. Some become previous-token heads, some become what eventually become induction heads, and a set of heads becomes specialized for these multigram patterns. You can see that in the refined LLC: certain heads' complexity, measured on data rich in those patterns, rises in a way that tracks them taking on this role.

The part I find most interesting is that the multigram circuit isn't static once it forms. It develops early, and then the induction circuit comes online. Induction is a more general, more compressed solution for a lot of in-context repetition that the model might otherwise have handled by memorizing particular sequences. After that you see signs of reorganization, where the multigram machinery interacts with the induction machinery and gets refined. It isn't simply "learn circuit A, then add circuit B." It's more like the model builds a somewhat memorization-heavy solution first, then a more general mechanism appears, and the earlier structure is partially restructured around it.

So the way I understand it is through a developmental lens. You get a sequence of stages, and the order matters. Some structures act as scaffolding, some become specialized, and some get compressed or repurposed later. A single snapshot of the final model would make it hard to see that history, but if you track these geometric measures through training, you can read some of it off.

There's a caveat: this is a small model, and our interpretations of what each head is doing are only as good as the data distributions and probes we use to condition the refined LLC. But it's suggestive that the same kind of story, differentiation, specialization, and then reorganization, shows up in larger models too. That's a big part of why we think studying development is a promising route to interpretability.

r003.rationale: It describes circuit reorganization but does not state that multigram behaviors move from the first layer to the second.

fable-5.1.text:
So the setup here is a small two-layer attention-only transformer trained on natural language, and the question we were asking is: can we see the model's internal structure develop over training, and can we tie that development to what's actually being learned? We used the local learning coefficient, the LLC, to look at this, and in particular we looked at refined versions of it where you restrict the data distribution or restrict which parts of the model you're measuring.

What we found with the multigram circuit is that it comes in stages, and those stages show up as distinct changes in the LLC curves. Early on, the model is essentially learning bigram statistics, just the frequencies of what token follows what. The LLC rises quickly during that phase. Then there's a period where the model starts picking up on n-gram statistics more generally, skip-trigrams, multigram structure, things where the prediction depends on a couple of earlier tokens rather than just the immediately preceding one. And what's interesting is that the LLC behaves somewhat non-monotonically across this transition. At one point it actually drops, which is a signature of the model simplifying, in the sense of moving to a region of parameter space with lower effective complexity, before it rises again as the induction circuit forms.

So the picture we ended up with is that the multigram machinery isn't a single thing that appears all at once. Different components, the first-layer heads, the second-layer heads, the embeddings, are contributing at different times, and if you compute per-component LLCs you can see which part is doing the work at each stage. Some of the second-layer heads, for instance, go through a phase of being specialized to multigram-type behavior before the induction circuit takes over and they get partially repurposed.

I'd stress that we're not claiming a full mechanistic account of every weight here. What we have is a developmental story, with the LLC acting as a kind of macroscopic probe that lets you say, "something structurally significant happened here," and then the data-restricted and weight-restricted versions let you localize that to particular behaviors and particular parts of the network. The multigram circuit was one of the clearest cases where that localization matched up nicely with what you'd expect from a more hand-done interpretability analysis.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a declining first-layer learning-coefficient signal with a one-layer n-gram baseline or interpret such a decline as loss of multigram-prediction information.

r003.rationale: It mentions second-layer heads being specialized and later partially repurposed, but does not state that multigram behaviors migrate from the first layer to the second.

r004.rationale: It does not describe emerging nested-pattern prediction as depending on information passed from first-layer heads to second-layer heads.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a process where relatively general-purpose components become coordinated into a more specific computation. A multigram circuit is doing something like predicting the next token from a short sequence of preceding tokens, rather than just from the current token.

In a two-layer Transformer, the first layer can move information about earlier tokens into the representation at a later position. The second layer can then use that information to make a prediction conditional on the combination. So the important development isn’t just that one attention head learns to look backward. It’s that the information it supplies becomes useful to a downstream component, and those components learn to work together.

That gives us a way to think about development at the level of the circuit: what computations are available early on, and when do they become integrated into a more capable computation? I’d distinguish that functional story from a complete causal explanation of why training takes that particular path. Identifying the circuit is a step toward that explanation, but it doesn’t, by itself, settle it.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I understand it is as a process of building up a circuit out of simpler components. A multigram circuit uses combinations of tokens in the context to help predict the next token, rather than just relying on the immediately preceding token.

In a two-layer Transformer, the first layer can move information about earlier tokens into the representation at a later position. The second layer can then use that information to recognize a pattern and make a prediction. So you have this division of labor: one layer prepares a useful representation, and the next layer reads it.

The interesting developmental question is how those pieces become coordinated. A component’s usefulness depends on what the other components are doing, so it’s not necessarily a matter of each part independently getting steadily better. You can have a period where the ingredients are developing without much visible improvement, followed by a relatively rapid change once they start working together. That’s the sense in which I think of the multigram circuit as an emergent computational structure.
